# Lynn Conway Summary
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer whose innovations revolutionized integrated circuit (chip) design. After earning degrees from Columbia University, she began her career at IBM in 1964, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling, laying groundwork for superscalar processor architecture. Following her public gender transition in 1968, Conway briefly faced career setbacks—including being fired from IBM—but relaunched her profession, eventually joining Xerox PARC. There, her work with Ivan Sutherland and Carver Mead led to the Mead–Conway VLSI chip design methodology, enabling the rapid prototyping and scalable design rules that transformed computing and electronics industries. The methodology, institutionalized via the MOSIS system, democratized chip design for universities and startups, sparking the growth of the foundry model and electronic design automation.
Conway became a professor at the University of Michigan, contributed to DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative, and retired as professor emerita in 1998. Widely recognized as a trailblazer, she received numerous honors, including fellowship in the IEEE, the Computer Pioneer Award, and induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame. Later in life, Conway became a prominent transgender rights activist, sharing her story to inspire others and advocating for LGBT inclusion in engineering societies. Her career memoirs, activism, and technical legacy have left an enduring impact on both computer science and diversity in STEM fields. Conway died in June 2024 at age 86.
